Thank you Mr. Speaker, colleagues. Today we heard, uh, quite articulately about how a key issue for Utah families across both the Wasatch Front and rural Utah is the cost of living.
And House Bill 29 affords us an opportunity to find a area of bipartisan support. And this is about tackling junk fees. Junk fees is defined as a mandatory fee that is not disclosed upfront.

So this isn't a utility fee where you are charged based on how much you use, and it's not a fee where you're choosing a different option when you're at the point of sale. These are about hidden fees that, that really mask the transparent cost to do business and to purchase things for consumers.

For example, ticket fees. How many of you have looked at, uh, to go to a concert or to a sporting event for, uh, let's say $75? But at the time that you're checking out that price is inflated to $125, not including tax, not including maybe things that you may have added, but these are fees that are mandatory.

You don't, it's not opt-in or opt out. That is deceptive pricing. President Trump's Federal Trade Commission has actually taken this on at the federal level. They have given states guidance to how to regulate and look at these junk fees.

So at the end of the day, when we're talking about the cost of living for some, for maybe something for about concert tickets, that could just be a couple dollars in your, in your pocket that wasn't there before. But when you look at families who are scraping paycheck to paycheck, working to make ends meet, take an apartment rental, for example, if they're advertised, let's say $1,200 for an apartment, and this family knows that that's
what they can fit in their family budget, only to find that after several weeks doing application fees, taking the time and the sweat equity to get to the point where they're ready to move in.
